title: Check the claim before reporting it, and make the record match by construction

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited f8d2c3d on top of d93f78e (bookkeeping). Sprint file read fresh immediately before this verdict; `git diff d93f78e HEAD -- docs/sprints/2-in-progress/` is empty, so no mid-build amendment. Working tree clean apart from the known-inert .vscode/settings.json.

Note on this audit's own footing: this sprint edits qa1.md, which is my instructions. I have not taken the new rule on faith because it is addressed to me — Req 3's criterion says exercise it, so I ran it against all three real instances that motivated it, including one from a sprint I passed. Results below.

================================================================
REQ 1 — THE WINDOW IS GENUINELY CLOSED, TRACED STEP BY STEP
================================================================

The criterion makes a remaining window a FAIL, so I traced every step between the push and the publish for anything that could move HEAD, rather than reading the prose and agreeing with it.

  step 6  push the audited commit          -> pushing creates no commit; HEAD unchanged.
  step 7  watch the pipeline               -> no repo mutation.
  step 8  /sprint-ship                     -> writes docs/sprints/state/sprint-N.json and nothing else.
                                              Grepped sprint_lifecycle.py for git mutations: the ONLY
                                              subprocess calls in the entire file are `git rev-parse`
                                              (four sites). No commit, add, checkout, tag or reset
                                              anywhere in the tool. HEAD cannot move here.
  step 9.1 scripts/verify-tarball.sh       -> grepped for git mutations: none. Packs and installs into
                                              a temp directory. HEAD unchanged.
  step 9.2 npm publish                     -> package.json has NO scripts block at all, so there is no
                                              prepack/prepare/prepublishOnly hook that could commit or
                                              tag. `npm publish` itself does not create commits.
  step 9.3 commit + push bookkeeping       -> after the publish, by construction.

So HEAD at publish time is the same commit pushed at step 6, which is the commit QA1 audited. gitHead is stamped from that. `last_shipped_commit` matches by construction and no reship correction is needed. The window is closed, not described better.

The tarball exclusion was verified, not assumed, and I verified it independently rather than accepting the handoff. Copied the repo, simulated step 8 by writing a phase change and last_shipped_commit into sprint-9.json plus a registry edit, confirmed with `git status --short` that both were genuinely uncommitted, then ran `npm pack`. The tarball's entire docs/sprints/ contents: seven .gitkeep files. Nothing else. Filtering the listing for any non-.gitkeep path under docs/sprints returns nothing. Publishing with the state file uncommitted is clean.

One correction to the rationale, not the instruction. Step 9.1 says running verify-tarball.sh uncommitted "tests the actual scenario the next step depends on, not a clean tree that would prove nothing about it." npm pack reads the working tree and ignores git status entirely, so a committed state file packs identically to an uncommitted one — a clean tree would in fact prove the same thing. The instruction is still right (run it there, on the real tree, before publishing) and the outcome is correct; only the "would prove nothing" clause overstates. Not worth a commit on its own; worth knowing before someone reasons from it.

================================================================
REQ 3 — EXERCISED AGAINST ALL THREE REAL INSTANCES, PLUS A CONTROL
================================================================

The criterion says a rule that would not have caught the three instances is not written correctly yet. Ran the exact check the new instruction prescribes:

  sprint 8's original criterion, 0.1.4 -> 0.1.6 for sprint 3's rule:
    git diff v0.1.4 v0.1.6 -- .claude/agents/qa1.md      => EMPTY  => CAUGHT
    git diff v0.1.4 v0.1.6 -- .claude/agents/pipeman.md  => EMPTY  => CAUGHT
  sprint 7's inherited criterion, 0.1.6 -> 0.1.7:
    git diff v0.1.6 v0.1.7 -- .claude/agents CLAUDE.md   => EMPTY  => CAUGHT
  CONTROL — a genuinely satisfiable pair must still pass, or the rule is just a blanket refusal:
    git diff v0.1.2 v0.1.6 -- .claude/agents/qa1.md      => 1 file changed, 2 insertions  => PASSES

The rule catches both real failures and does not fire on the pair that actually works. It is written correctly. It is also written in the right place — folded into the existing fresh-reread step rather than added as a ninth thing to remember, which is what makes it likely to actually run.

Applied it to this sprint's own criteria while I was there, since a fourth instance is the obvious way to fail: sprint 9's LiveQA criterion deliberately names no version pair and instructs LiveQA to choose one against git diff. That removes the defect by not specifying the thing that keeps going wrong, which is the correct fix. And a satisfiable pair does exist for LiveQA to find — `git diff v0.1.7 HEAD -- .claude/agents/` shows all three files changed, so 0.1.7 -> 0.1.8 works.

================================================================
REQS 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 AND THE TARBALL CRITERION — MET
================================================================

Req 2 — MET. Step 10 instructs `npm view <pkg>@<version> gitHead` and to report that value, "never from what you meant to ship", and the same caveat is repeated inline in the output format's new field. It does not permit reporting an intended commit; it names the registry as the source in both places a reader would look. Correct that this stays even with Req 1 closing the usual gap — a check that only runs when you expect it to fail is not a check.

Req 4 — MET, read cold. It tells Master Controller what to do instead, not merely what to avoid: if a criterion is genuinely blocked, say so with what was attempted and what failed. It cites sprint 7's actual false claim as the concrete instance and states why this failure mode is worse than a wrong requirement (a wrong requirement gets caught downstream; an unattempted impossibility claim removes the check and nobody finds out). That reasoning is the part that will make it stick.

Req 5 — MET, and message-only proven mechanically. Filtered the install.js diff for any added or removed line that is not a comment: exactly two removed and two added, all four inside the returned template string. No condition, no branch, no helper touched. The message now says "since the version you have", which is what hasUpstreamChangedSinceInstall actually establishes.
  Your judgment call on the fallback path is right and I would have made the same one. The fallback ("changed anywhere in known history", used only when there is no baseline for the exact installed version) does not strictly establish "since the version you have" — but it only fires for installs with no version marker or a version outside the table, it already errs toward the real-conflict message, and Req 5's criterion explicitly wants a message-only edit. Threading a third message variant through would have broken that criterion to fix a case that is rarer than the imprecision. Flagging it rather than deciding it silently was the right call; the answer is leave it.

Req 6 — MET. package.json 0.1.8, one line.

Req 7 — MET, run not read. `node scripts/launcher_test.js` -> 74 OK lines, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. The assertion is by condition, not by string presence: one test seeds an install where upstream did NOT change the file and asserts the message is ABSENT (doesNotMatch), the other seeds a real upstream change and asserts it PRESENT. Both directions covered, so neither a stuck-on nor a stuck-off message survives.
  The qa1.md -> liveqa.md switch in the baseline test is correct and does not weaken it. Sprint 9 edits qa1.md's live content, so its current bytes no longer match any row in the committed baseline table; a test proving "matches a published baseline" needs a file this repo has not since changed, and liveqa.md is untouched since 0.1.5. Switching the fixture rather than touching the baseline table was the right instinct — the alternative would have been regenerating generated data to make a test pass, which is how a wrong hash gets into that file.

TARBALL CRITERION — MET, AND CHECKED HARDER THAN VERIFY-TARBALL DOES. scripts/verify-tarball.sh: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, 0.1.8, launcher files match live source, docs/sprints clean, baseline table present with 7 paths. Then, separately, packed the real tarball and confirmed all three modified agent files are present AND carry the new content AND are byte-identical to this repo's source: qa1.md's version-pair rule, pipeman.md's gitHead instruction, master-controller.md's untestability boundary — each found in the packed copy, each cmp-identical. This sprint will not ship as a no-op.

================================================================
YOUR QUESTION: THE RESHIP/REPUBLISH GAP
================================================================

Worth a note to Master Controller, not a sprint, and you were right not to build it. But the answer is more specific than "wait for a recurrence", so record this rather than just the yes/no.

npm versions are immutable, so a fix that has to reach users during the LiveQA loop cannot be republished at the same version — it forces a bump. That means the case isn't exotic: it is what happens the first time LiveQA FAILs a release sprint in a way the fix has to reach the registry for. It has genuinely not happened yet — sprint 6's and sprint 8's "reships" were record corrections, not republishes, which is exactly the defect Req 1 removes.

The specific thing to hand Master Controller is that step 9's trigger would not fire in that case. It keys on "a `package.json` version bump in the sprint's requirements", and a mid-fix-loop bump is by definition not in the sprint's requirements — it is a consequence of the fix. So the reship path would take step 8's "for anything else, commit and push it now" branch, move HEAD, and reintroduce the stale gitHead this sprint exists to remove. Req 2's registry check would catch it after the fact, which is the design working, but the ordering guard would not have applied.

That is consistent with this project's stated policy of building gates after a recurrence rather than pre-emptively, and I am not asking for it here. It is worth being on the record with the mechanism named, so that when it does happen nobody has to rediscover why.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL — NOT REQUIRED FIXES
================================================================

1. THE BASELINE TABLE IS TWO RELEASES STALE, and this sprint's release makes it three. scripts/baselines/user-owned-content.json covers 0.1.0-0.1.5, generatedAt 2026-08-31; the registry now serves through 0.1.7. Sprint 8's generator comment says to re-run it "whenever a new version publishes", and nothing in pipeman.md's release process says to — including the process this sprint just rewrote.
   No user is harmed today: every 0.1.6+ install writes a manifest, and the manifest branch wins outright, so baselines are only consulted for installs that predate 0.1.6, which the table does cover. The exposure is narrow and slow-growing — an install with no manifest and no version marker (a copied repo rather than an npx install) matching 0.1.6/0.1.7 content would conflict where it should be proven. But the drift is monotonic and the fix is one command, and the natural place for it is the release process this sprint is already editing. Master Controller's call whether that is a line in pipeman.md or a sprint.

2. Step 8 does not say WHICH commit to pass to /sprint-ship. If Pipeman squashes at step 5 and then records the pre-squash hash, last_shipped_commit and gitHead disagree again — not because HEAD moved before publish (it didn't, so this is not a Req 1 failure) but because the recorded value was never HEAD. Req 2's registry check catches it, which is what Req 2 is for. A clause saying "the commit you actually pushed, which is HEAD" would prevent rather than detect it. Historically this project has not squashed, so this is hypothetical.

3. Step 9.1's "a clean tree would prove nothing about it" rationale, above under Req 1.

CODE QUALITY

Test coverage: 74 passing; the new assertions test both directions of the condition rather than the presence of a string.
Error handling: no error paths touched.
Standards: message-only code change proven mechanically; the test fixture switched rather than the generated data it depends on; bookkeeping split from substance for the eighth sprint running; the self-caught draft error in step 9.3 (ship never closes a sprint) was correct to fix — /sprint-complete is Dev Team's and happens later, and the original wording would have put a second HEAD-moving commit inside the window.
Security: no security surface.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 9, then Pipeman ships --commit f8d2c3d specifically — this PASS records that commit's tree, and if bookkeeping lands on top first, HEAD moves and /sprint-ship will refuse. Then follow the new step 9 order exactly: verify-tarball with the state write uncommitted, publish, and only then commit the bookkeeping. This release is the first test of the reorder, and its own gitHead is the evidence for whether Req 1 worked.

For LiveQA: 0.1.7 -> 0.1.8 is a satisfiable pair, confirmed by git diff on all three agent files. Verify it yourself before running, as the criterion instructs — that instruction exists because three sprints running got this wrong, and taking my word for it would defeat the point.

CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.8, no browser (the package is the product). Environment: macOS, npx against the live registry, scratch targets /tmp/fc9-up, /tmp/fc9-a, /tmp/fc9-b, /tmp/fc9-c, /tmp/fc9-e, /tmp/fc9-f, /tmp/fc9-fresh, 2026-09-01.

Req 1 works and is verified — the publish reorder does exactly what it was written to do. The conditional is on Req 5, the sprint's only code change, which shipped a message that is demonstrably false to every install at 0.1.6 or later. Details below.

================================================================
CRITERION 1 — REGISTRY AND gitHead, EXPECTED TO MATCH FIRST TIME: PASS. REQ 1 WORKS.
================================================================
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.8. `npm view fully-completely@0.1.8 gitHead` -> f8d2c3dbe071cf51aa5673ec05c115a0a015a7ff, an exact match for last_shipped_commit.

The stronger fact, which is what Req 1 actually claims: the published gitHead is the AUDITED commit, not a bookkeeping commit on top of it. QA1's recorded qa1_audited_tree_hash is c9772ec8aa4eb5f0cf57a1306c46a74a89f8e050 and `git rev-parse f8d2c3d^{tree}` is c9772ec8aa4eb5f0cf57a1306c46a74a89f8e050 — identical. In sprints 6, 7 and 8 the published gitHead was always the ship-bookkeeping commit and the trees differed; here they are the same object.

And the history proves no correction was needed rather than me taking it on report: sprint 9's state history contains a single `pipeman shipped commit=f8d2c3d` event and NO `reshipped` event. Sprints 6, 7 and 8 all have one. The record matched by construction on the first attempt, which is the requirement's stated success condition.

================================================================
CRITERION 2 — THE AGENT-FILE CHANGES REACH A REAL INSTALL: PASS.
================================================================
The criterion deliberately names no version pair and makes choosing one LiveQA's call, against the diff. I verified satisfiability BEFORE running, in both directions.

git: `git diff --stat e91dd2f f8d2c3d` shows pipeman.md (+9/-4), qa1.md (+1/-1), master-controller.md (+1).
Published tarballs, which is what actually ships:
  .claude/agents/pipeman.md            88a9c64a8ff4 -> 16ecdbe5c464   DIFFERS
  .claude/agents/qa1.md                95f7bf134eef -> f2b0914363e4   DIFFERS
  .claude/agents/master-controller.md  f7f62ea455ff -> aee4860a6771   DIFFERS
  .claude/agents/liveqa.md             15d0e606ca5e -> 15d0e606ca5e   SAME
So 0.1.7 -> 0.1.8 is a satisfiable pair for all three files under test. Recording the method because this is the check sprint 9's own Req 3 adds, and it is the first sprint where the pair was confirmed before use rather than after.

Installed published 0.1.7, left all files untouched, upgraded to published 0.1.8. Each change absent before (grep 0) and present after (grep 1):
  pipeman.md            "Establish `gitHead` from the registry, never from what you meant to ship"   0 -> 1
  qa1.md                "is only a valid criterion if the file under test actually differs"          0 -> 1
  master-controller.md  "A false claim of untestability is more dangerous"                           0 -> 1
Backups written for all three plus install.js (.fc-bak-0.1.7), and confirmed the backups hold the OLD content (pipeman.md.fc-bak-0.1.7 has 0 occurrences of the new text). Manifest refreshed to 7 entries. Exit 0.

This is the epic's whole thesis working: three process-rule changes, written as agent-file prose, reached an existing install through a published upgrade. Before 0.1.6 none of them could have.

================================================================
CRITERION 3 — BOTH CONFLICT MESSAGES STILL BEHAVE: FAIL. THIS IS THE CONDITIONAL.
================================================================

FINDING (blocking) — the tightened Req 5 message makes a false claim to every install at 0.1.6 or later.

Demonstrated, from real published artifacts:
  Installed published 0.1.7. Edited .claude/agents/liveqa.md. Upgraded to published 0.1.8.
  Message, verbatim: "...This file's shipped content has changed since the version you have; to see
  exactly what's different in the current release, run `npx fully-completely` again inside an empty
  scratch directory to get a fresh copy, then diff it against your own file and merge anything you
  want by hand."

liveqa.md did not change between 0.1.7 and 0.1.8. Both published tarballs hash to 15d0e606ca5e. The statement is false, and it sends the reader to diff a file whose only difference is their own edit — the precise failure QA1 blocked sprint 8's round 1 for ("Round 1's version sent five people to look at nothing").

This is a REGRESSION INTRODUCED BY THIS SPRINT, not an inherited defect, and I checked rather than assumed. Same scenario one release earlier: installed published 0.1.6, edited liveqa.md, upgraded to published 0.1.7. That message read "...has changed since it was first published" — which is TRUE of liveqa.md, since it did change between 0.1.0 and 0.1.3. Req 5 replaced a true-but-vague claim with a specific one the installer cannot substantiate. The requirement's own premise — that the condition "actually established the stronger and more useful 'since the version you have'" — is incorrect. It does not establish that whenever the installed version is outside the baseline table.

ROOT CAUSE — THE BASELINE TABLE IS STALE AND NOTHING REGENERATES IT.
scripts/baselines/user-owned-content.json in the published 0.1.8 covers versions ['0.1.0','0.1.1','0.1.2','0.1.3','0.1.4','0.1.5'] and carries generatedAt 2026-08-31T22:32:54.449Z — byte-identical to the table 0.1.6 shipped. It has never been regenerated. Not covered: 0.1.6, 0.1.7, 0.1.8.

Control, which isolates the cause rather than asserting it: installed published 0.1.5 (a version the table DOES cover), edited liveqa.md, upgraded to 0.1.8. Correct message: "There's no upstream update pending for this file — if it looks different from what we'd install, that difference is entirely your own edit, not something we changed. Nothing to reconcile; no action needed unless you want one." Same file, same edit, same target version; the only variable is whether the installed version has a baseline entry. So the message-selection logic is sound and the data behind it is stale.

scripts/baselines/generate.js is committed and shipped, exactly as sprint 8's Req 2 required so the table "extends to future releases." Nothing runs it. pipeman.md's newly rewritten release order — which this sprint expanded in detail — contains zero occurrences of "baseline". Every future release inherits this and the uncovered range grows by one version each time.

SCOPE, STATED FAIRLY. This is a message defect, not a destructive one, and I confirmed the safe branch is unaffected:
 - Untouched user-owned files in a 0.1.6/0.1.7 install still upgrade correctly. Installed 0.1.7 clean, upgraded to 0.1.8: 0 conflicts, 4 files replaced, manifest 7 entries. Those installs carry a manifest (written by the 0.1.6+ installer), so manifest proof applies and baselines are never consulted.
 - Nothing is overwritten that should not be. Sprint 6's safety property is untouched by this.
 - The false claim reaches only the case where a user EDITED a user-owned file and their installed version is 0.1.6 or later.
So: nobody loses work, and some people are told to go and diff a file that has no diff.

REQUIRED FIX — two parts, and I would not accept the first alone:
 1. Regenerate scripts/baselines/user-owned-content.json to cover 0.1.6 and 0.1.7 (and 0.1.8 as it publishes). generate.js already exists for this.
 2. Add regenerating it to pipeman.md's release order, or make the message degrade honestly when the installed version has no baseline entry. Without one of these the table goes stale again on the very next release and this finding returns. Wording and mechanism are Dev Team's; what must be true afterwards is that no install is told upstream changed a file that upstream did not change.

Which of the two is the real fix is arguably Master Controller's call, since "the message must not claim what it cannot establish" is a requirement-level property and Req 5 as written asserts the opposite. Flagging that rather than deciding it.

================================================================
CRITERION 4 — FRESH INSTALL: PASS
================================================================
`npx -y fully-completely@0.1.8` into an empty directory: "Installed 0.1.8 (first install)", 45 files, exit 0, manifest 7 entries, 0 non-.gitkeep files under docs/sprints.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Everything above I ran and observed directly on macOS against the live registry. Every message quoted came from a real `npx` upgrade between two published versions, never from reading install.js. The regression-vs-inherited question was settled by running the 0.1.6 -> 0.1.7 case, not by reasoning about the diff. Pipeman's claim that gitHead matched with no correction was verified against both the registry and the absence of a reship event in the state history, and this round it was true.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Do not close sprint 9. Fix the baseline staleness and the message that depends on it, then reship and I will re-test.

What should not be disturbed: Req 1 is correct and verified, and it is the most valuable thing in this release — three consecutive sprints needed a post-hoc reship to make the record honest and this one did not. Reqs 2, 3 and 4 all reached a real install. Keep them.

The irony is worth stating plainly rather than leaving for someone to notice later: this sprint exists to stop roles reporting states they have not established, and its single code change made the installer assert something it cannot establish. The three process fixes landed; the one code fix reproduced the defect they were written to prevent. That is not a reason to doubt the sprint's premise — it is the premise, demonstrated once more, and this time the check caught it before a user did.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Live-tested published npm 0.1.9, no browser (the package is the product). Environment: macOS, npx against the live registry, scratch targets /tmp/fc9r-a (the round-1 repro), /tmp/fc9r-b, /tmp/fc9r-c, /tmp/fc9r-d, /tmp/fc9r-f, /tmp/fc9r-s, /tmp/fc9r-u, 2026-09-01.

Round 1's blocking finding is fixed, verified against published artifacts rather than against Dev Team's local build. Both halves of the required fix landed and both are demonstrated below.

PROVENANCE — VERIFIED
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.9; dist-tags latest -> 0.1.9; `npm view fully-completely@0.1.9 gitHead` -> 87d9f55c28640161abc78a9ceb02171eacc43d3e, an exact match for last_shipped_commit. Remote tag v0.1.9 dereferences to the same commit. The reship is recorded in state history (`pipeman reshipped commit=87d9f55`). The publish-order fix from round 1 held on a reship as well as on an original ship.

NOTED, NOT A GATE ISSUE: 87d9f55's tree is 453da882785cc879d94344ab821d4c4597e3ce96; QA1's recorded qa1_audited_tree_hash is c9772ec8aa4eb5f0cf57a1306c46a74a89f8e050. They differ, because this is a LiveQA-loop fix and `cmd_reship` deliberately permits shipping a commit gate 1 has not audited. That is documented, intended behaviour, not a violation. Recording it because sprint 7 shipped the live-loop audit record specifically so an audit of exactly this kind of fix could be put on the record, and no `live_loop_audit` event exists in sprint 9's history — the mechanism exists and went unused on the first fix that qualified for it. That is Master Controller's and QA1's call, not mine, and it does not affect this verdict.

ROUND-1 FINDING — FIXED. THE EXACT REPRO NOW BEHAVES.
Round 1's blocker: a published 0.1.7 install with an edited `.claude/agents/liveqa.md`, upgraded to 0.1.8, was told "This file's shipped content has changed since the version you have" when liveqa.md was byte-identical across those releases.

Precondition re-established from the published tarballs rather than assumed — liveqa.md is 15d0e606ca5e9847 in 0.1.7, 0.1.8 AND 0.1.9, so "no update pending" is the factually correct answer:
  Installed published 0.1.7, edited liveqa.md, upgraded to published 0.1.9.
  Message, verbatim: "...There's no upstream update pending for this file — if it looks different from
  what we'd install, that difference is entirely your own edit, not something we changed. Nothing to
  reconcile; no action needed unless you want one."
The false claim is gone. My edit survived (grep 1), exit 0.

ALL FOUR MESSAGE CONDITIONS, EACH PRODUCED FROM A REAL PUBLISHED PAIR
I did not test only the fixed case. The risk with a message-selection fix is that it over-corrects and starts hedging when it does know, so I produced every branch:

A. Installed version covered, file NOT changed upstream (0.1.7 -> 0.1.9, liveqa.md, 15d0e606 both ends)
   -> "There's no upstream update pending for this file..."   CORRECT, and this is round 1's defect.

B. Installed version covered, file GENUINELY changed upstream (0.1.7 -> 0.1.9, pipeman.md, 88a9c64a -> 16ecdbe5)
   -> "This file's shipped content has changed since the version you have; to see exactly what's
       different in the current release, run `npx fully-completely` again..."   CORRECT and TRUE.
   This is the case that matters for over-correction: the precise wording is still used where the
   installer can actually substantiate it. Req 5's intent survives the fix.

C. Control, a version covered by the table all along (0.1.5 -> 0.1.9, liveqa.md edited)
   -> "There's no upstream update pending for this file..."   CORRECT, unchanged from before. No regression
   on the path that was already working.

D. Installed version with NO baseline entry — the fallback branch. Simulated a future release by
   forcing the version marker to 0.0.9, outside the table's 0.1.0-0.1.8 coverage, in an otherwise real
   0.1.7 install with liveqa.md edited.
   -> "This file's shipped content has changed at some point since it was first published — this
       installer doesn't have exact data for the version you're on to say precisely when; to see
       exactly what's different in the current release, run `npx fully-completely` again..."
   This is the right answer and it is worth being explicit about why. It states what it knows (the file
   did change at some point since first publication — true), it names its own limitation instead of
   guessing, and it does NOT assert "since the version you have". Read cold, a user learns both what
   the installer established and what it could not. That is the property this sprint's whole epic is
   about, applied to the message that was violating it.

Branch D is the durable half of the fix and the reason I asked for it rather than accepting the table
regeneration alone: the table will go stale again the moment a release ships without regenerating it,
and when it does, the message degrades to an honest hedge instead of reverting to a falsehood.

BASELINE TABLE — REGENERATED, AND VERIFIED BY RECOMPUTING RATHER THAN READING
The shipped table in published 0.1.9 now covers ['0.1.0'..'0.1.8'], generatedAt 2026-09-01T06:22:21.049Z, up from the stale 0.1.0-0.1.5 that still carried 0.1.6's timestamp. Coverage now reaches the release immediately prior to this one.

A wrong hash in this table silently overwrites an edited file, and the three newly added versions are new data, so I rebuilt the whole thing from outside: fetched all nine published tarballs (0.1.0 through 0.1.8) and recomputed the CRLF-normalised sha256 of all seven tracked paths in every version.

  MATCHING: 63    MISMATCHED: 0    MISSING: 0    TOTAL: 63

Every hash, including all 21 newly added (7 paths x 0.1.6/0.1.7/0.1.8), corresponds to real published content. Done independently of scripts/baselines/generate.js — I hashed the tarballs directly, so a bug in the generator would not have hidden from this check.

REGRESSIONS — NONE. THE SAFETY PROPERTIES STILL HOLD.
Sprint 6's non-negotiable property, re-run against the new release: planted SENTINEL-S9R2-MUST-SURVIVE in .claude/agents/qa1.md in a published-0.1.4 install (no manifest, pre-manifest shape), upgraded to 0.1.9. Sentinel survived (grep 1), qa1.md sha256 IDENTICAL before and after (83e2ccc8cf0bcaef both sides), and the file was correctly EXCLUDED from the manifest — 6 entries, not 7, because an edited file matched nothing and is not proven untouched. Neither the message fix nor the regenerated table made the destructive branch reachable.

Untouched upgrade path: published 0.1.7 clean -> 0.1.9 produced 0 conflicts, 4 files replaced with backups, manifest refreshed to 7 entries, exit 0.
